questions.stem: Which structure does a bacterial cell LACK?

options.text: A nucleus enclosed by a membrane
options.explanation: Prokaryotes keep their DNA loose in the cytoplasm.
The wall is a named bacterial feature.
Plasmids are named bacterial DNA elements.
Cytoplasm is named as present.

questions.stem: Which list gives the structures a bacterial cell POSSESSES?

options.explanation: Neither nucleus nor chloroplast exists here.

options.text: Cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, plasmids
options.explanation: This is exactly the inventory the note lists.
No nucleus exists in bacteria.
Mitochondria are absent from bacteria.

questions.stem: Why are bacteria described as prokaryotic rather than eukaryotic?

options.text: Because they lack a cell wall
options.explanation: They actually have a wall.
Lactobacillus is useful, so harm is not universal.

options.text: Because their genetic material sits loose in the cytoplasm with no enclosing membrane
options.explanation: The missing nucleus is the deciding contrast.
Size does not decide the classification.

questions.stem: Which pairing of example bacterium and role is correct?

options.explanation: The two roles are swapped.
Mucor is a fungus, not a bacterium.
Yeast is a fungus and TMV is a virus.

options.text: Lactobacillus bulgaricus — yoghurt production; Pneumococcus — pneumonia
options.explanation: Both named examples pair correctly with their roles.

questions.stem: What is the shape of the bacterial chromosome described in this note?

options.text: A single circular chromosome of DNA
options.explanation: The note names a circular chromosome.

options.text: Several linear chromosomes inside a nucleus
options.explanation: Both the shape and the location are wrong.
Plasmids ride alongside the main chromosome, they are not the whole genome.

options.text: No DNA at all, only RNA
options.explanation: Bacteria carry DNA; RNA-only describes some viruses.

questions.stem: State where the genetic material of a prokaryotic cell is found.
questions.modelAnswer: Loose in the cytoplasm, with no enclosing nuclear membrane.

questions.stem: Name the extra DNA elements a bacterial cell carries besides its chromosome.
questions.modelAnswer: Plasmids — small loops of DNA in the cytoplasm.

questions.stem: Explain why mitochondria cannot be drawn on a labelled bacterial cell diagram.
questions.modelAnswer: Bacteria lack mitochondria and every other membrane-bound organelle; their energy-releasing chemistry runs directly across the cell membrane and in the cytoplasm, so any diagram showing a mitochondrion has drawn a eukaryotic feature on a prokaryotic cell.

questions.stem: A pupil's labelled bacterial cell diagram includes plasmids, a cell wall and a nucleus. The plasmids and wall are correct — what must change, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: The nucleus must be removed and replaced by DNA loose in the cytoplasm (a circular chromosome), because bacteria are prokaryotes with no membrane-enclosed nucleus.
